title: Fourier series
summary: Say what a Fourier series is and why it exists; write its three forms and convert between them; compute coefficients for a sum of cosines without calculus by using orthogonality; draw the magnitude spectrum.

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **The claim** Take any periodic wave — a vowel, a square wave, a triangle wave — with fundamental frequency F₀ (period T₀ = 1/F₀). Fourier's theorem: you can build it exactly by adding sinusoids whose frequencies are **whole-number multiples of F₀**: F₀, 2F₀, 3F₀, … (the **harmonics**), each with its own amplitude and phase. Going from the wave to the list of amplitudes and phases is **Fourier analysis**; going back is **Fourier synthesis**. The list *is* the spectrum from Chapter 0.
blocks.slide: Any periodic wave is a sum of sinusoids

blocks.md: Why would that be true? Intuition: a periodic wave repeats every T₀. Any sinusoid at kF₀ also repeats every T₀ (it completes exactly k cycles). So the harmonics are exactly the set of 'ingredients' that share the wave's period; Fourier showed they're enough. Lab 4 Q5 is this in action — add more harmonics of a triangle wave and the sum gets closer and closer.

- x(t) is real-valued (pressure is real).
- It's periodic with fundamental period T₀ and fundamental frequency F₀ = 1/T₀.
- It's piecewise smooth. At a jump (a square wave's edge) the series converges to the midpoint of the two sides.

sections.heading: Three ways to write the same series

blocks.title: (1) is the intuitive one: a sum of cosines with amplitudes and phases. (2) splits each cosine into a cosine and a sine with no phase. (3) uses complex spinners at positive AND negative frequencies.
blocks.body:
(1) amplitude-phase:   x(t) = A₀ + Σ_{k=1}^{∞} A_k cos(2πF₀kt + ϕ_k)

(2) sine-cosine:       x(t) = a₀ + Σ_{k=1}^{∞} [ a_k cos(2πF₀kt) + b_k sin(2πF₀kt) ]

(3) exponential:       x(t) = Σ_{k=−∞}^{∞} X_k e^{j2πF₀kt}        X_k complex,  X_{−k} = X̄_k

blocks.md: k is the harmonic number. The k-th term is a cosine at frequency k·F₀ with amplitude A_k and phase ϕ_k — exactly the formula from Chapter 0, once per harmonic. A₀ is the constant offset (the average level); the note shows it's the k = 0 term with ϕ₀ = 0, since cos(0) = 1.

blocks.title: Converting amplitude-phase ↔ sine-cosine
blocks.body:
Show A_k cos(2πF₀kt + ϕ_k) = a_k cos(2πF₀kt) + b_k sin(2πF₀kt).

1. The sum formula: cos(α + β) = cos α cos β − sin α sin β. Let α = 2πF₀kt, β = ϕ_k.
2. A_k cos(α + ϕ_k) = A_k cos ϕ_k · cos α − A_k sin ϕ_k · sin α.
3. Match with a_k cos α + b_k sin α: **a_k = A_k cos ϕ_k**, **b_k = −A_k sin ϕ_k**.
4. Going back: a_k² + b_k² = A_k²(cos² + sin²) = A_k², so **A_k = √(a_k² + b_k²)**. And −b_k/a_k = tan ϕ_k, so **ϕ_k = atan2(−b_k, a_k)** (atan2 picks the right quadrant).
5. Lab 4 Q4-style check: for a wave with only cosine terms (b_k = 0), ϕ_k = 0 and A_k = a_k.
blocks.slide: Why (1) and (2) are the same: the cosine sum formula

blocks.title: Converting to the exponential form
blocks.body:
Show each cosine becomes a pair of complex spinners.

1. Chapter 4: cos θ = (e^{jθ} + e^{−jθ})/2 and sin θ = (e^{jθ} − e^{−jθ})/(2j).
2. So a_k cos(2πF₀kt) + b_k sin(2πF₀kt) = [(a_k − jb_k)/2]·e^{j2πF₀kt} + [(a_k + jb_k)/2]·e^{−j2πF₀kt}.
3. Read off: **X_k = (a_k − jb_k)/2** for k > 0, **X_{−k} = (a_k + jb_k)/2** — conjugates, as promised. X₀ = a₀ = A₀.
4. From form (1) directly: **X_k = (A_k/2)·e^{jϕ_k}**, so **A_k = 2|X_k|** and **ϕ_k = ∠X_k**. Half the amplitude at +kF₀, half at −kF₀ — Chapter 4's result, one harmonic at a time.
blocks.slide: Why (2)/(1) and (3) are the same: Euler

rows: a_k = A_k cos ϕ_k;  b_k = −A_k sin ϕ_k
X_k = (a_k − jb_k)/2;  X_{−k} = (a_k + jb_k)/2;  X₀ = a₀
X_k = A_k e^{jϕ_k}/2;  X_{−k} = A_k e^{−jϕ_k}/2;  X₀ = A₀

blocks.prompt: Lab 4 Q7: for 2cos(2πF₀t + π/2), find X₁ and X₋₁.
blocks.answer: X₁ = (A/2)e^{jϕ} = 1·e^{jπ/2} = j (since e^{jπ/2} = cos π/2 + j sin π/2 = j). X₋₁ = conjugate = −j. Check with the a,b route: a₁ = 2cos(π/2) = 0, b₁ = −2sin(π/2) = −2 → X₁ = (0 − j(−2))/2 = j. ✓

sections.heading: Finding the coefficients: multiply, integrate, normalize

blocks.md: Given a wave, how do you find how much of harmonic k it contains? **Multiply x(t) by the harmonic you're testing for, integrate over one period, and divide by the period.** The result is nonzero only if x(t) actually contains that harmonic. It's a detector.

blocks.title: For (2): note the 2/T₀ on a_k and b_k but 1/T₀ on a₀. For (3): multiply by the spinner with the OPPOSITE frequency (−k).
blocks.body:
a₀ = (1/T₀) ∫₀^{T₀} x(t) dt                        (the average)
a_k = (2/T₀) ∫₀^{T₀} x(t) cos(2πF₀kt) dt
b_k = (2/T₀) ∫₀^{T₀} x(t) sin(2πF₀kt) dt

X_k = (1/T₀) ∫₀^{T₀} x(t) e^{−j2πF₀kt} dt

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **The one fact that makes Fourier analysis possible** A sinusoid with no offset, integrated over a whole number of its own cycles, gives **zero** — every positive hump cancels a negative hump. So when you multiply x(t) (a sum of harmonics) by cos(2πF₀kt) and integrate, every product of two *different* harmonics is itself a sum of sinusoids at nonzero frequencies and integrates to zero. Only the product of harmonic k with itself survives — cos² has a positive average of ½, giving T₀/2 (hence the 2/T₀ in front). The harmonics are **orthogonal**: the test for k ignores everything that isn't k.

blocks.title: Why X_k = (1/T₀)∫ x(t) e^{−j2πF₀kt} dt
blocks.body:
Substitute the series for x(t) and watch everything but one term vanish.

1. ∫₀^{T₀} x(t) e^{−j2πF₀kt} dt = ∫ Σ_n X_n e^{j2πF₀nt} e^{−j2πF₀kt} dt.
2. Swap sum and integral: Σ_n X_n ∫ e^{j2πF₀(n−k)t} dt.
3. If n ≠ k, the integrand is a complex sinusoid at a nonzero frequency over T₀/|n−k| — whole cycles — so it integrates to 0.
4. If n = k, the exponent is 0, the integrand is the constant X_k, and the integral is X_k·T₀.
5. So the whole thing equals X_k·T₀. Divide by T₀: X_k = (1/T₀)∫ x(t) e^{−j2πF₀kt} dt.
blocks.slide: The derivation in Koo's note, §4.1 (for the exam's 'why')

blocks.md: **Magnitude spectrum**: A_k (or 2|X_k|) at each frequency k·F₀ — stems at F₀, 2F₀, 3F₀… **Phase spectrum**: ϕ_k = ∠X_k at each k·F₀. In the two-sided (exponential) picture, the stems are |X_k| at both +kF₀ and −kF₀, each half as tall.

blocks.title: x(t) = 0.4 + cos(2π·2t + π/4) + 0.6cos(2π·5t − π/2)
blocks.body:
Write the two-sided coefficients.

1. F₀ = 1 Hz (harmonics at 2 and 5 are both multiples of 1). Three components: k = 0, 2, 5.
2. X₀ = A₀ = 0.4.
3. k = 2: A = 1, ϕ = π/4 → X₂ = 0.5·e^{jπ/4} = 0.354 + 0.354j; X₋₂ = 0.354 − 0.354j. |X| = 0.5, ∠ = ±π/4.
4. k = 5: A = 0.6, ϕ = −π/2 → X₅ = 0.3·e^{−jπ/2} = −0.3j; X₋₅ = +0.3j. |X| = 0.3, ∠ = ∓π/2.
5. Magnitude spectrum (one-sided): 0.4 at 0 Hz, 1 at 2 Hz, 0.6 at 5 Hz. Phase spectrum: 0, π/4, −π/2.

blocks.title: F₀ = 5 Hz triangle wave with cosine amplitudes 8/(π²k²) for odd k
blocks.body:
The lab's first block of questions.

1. Q1: F₀ = 5 Hz → T₀ = 1/5 = 0.2 s.
2. Q2: 5th harmonic is at 5·F₀ = 25 Hz.
3. Q3: its amplitude is 8/(π²·25) = 8/(25π²). Even harmonics are 0 (a triangle wave is symmetric in a way that kills them).
4. Q4 (the sketch): stems at 5, 15, 25, 35, 45 Hz with heights 8/π², 8/(9π²), 8/(25π²), 8/(49π²), 8/(81π²) — falling fast — and nothing at 10, 20, 30, 40 Hz.
5. Q5 (essay): as you add terms, the straight sides get straighter and the rounded peaks get sharper; the remaining error is largest at the peaks and troughs, because sharp corners need the highest harmonics.
6. Q12: two-sided coefficients X_k = A_k/2 = 4/(π²k²) for odd k > 0, zero for even k.
7. Q13: rebuilding from X_k should **match** the cosine reconstruction, since each ±k pair of complex terms adds up to exactly the k-th cosine.
blocks.slide: Lab 4 Q1–Q5, Q12–Q13: the triangle wave

blocks.prompt: x(t) = 4cos(2π·10t − π/3). Give X₁ and X₋₁ (F₀ = 10 Hz) and the one-sided magnitude spectrum.
blocks.answer: X₁ = 2e^{−jπ/3} = 1 − j√3; X₋₁ = 2e^{jπ/3} = 1 + j√3. Magnitude spectrum: one stem of height 4 at 10 Hz (or two stems of height 2 at ±10 Hz two-sided). Phase −π/3 at 10 Hz.

blocks.body: A periodic signal written as a sum of harmonically related sinusoids (frequencies kF₀). Coefficients come from multiplying by the harmonic, integrating over one period, and normalizing; orthogonality makes each test isolate one harmonic. Two-sided coefficient X_k has |X_k| = A_k/2 and ∠X_k = ϕ_k.

exercises.title: Coefficients without calculus
exercises.prompt: x(t) = 3 + 4·cos(2π·10·t) + 2·cos(2π·30·t + π/2). Period? Fundamental frequency? Write the trigonometric-form coefficients (a₀, aₖ, bₖ) for all k, and the complex coefficients Xₖ for k = 0, ±1, ±3. Then sketch the magnitude spectrum.
hints: The fundamental is the largest F that divides all the frequencies present: 10 and 30 → 10 Hz. Period = 1/10 s. The 30 Hz term is harmonic k = 3.
Two traps: forgetting that the constant 3 is the k = 0 term, and mishandling the +π/2 phase — cos(θ + π/2) = −sin θ, so that term is a *sine*, which lands in bₖ, with a sign.
Complex form: a cosine of amplitude A at harmonic k splits into Xₖ = X₋ₖ = A/2 (the two spinners). With a phase ϕ: Xₖ = (A/2)e^(jϕ), X₋ₖ = (A/2)e^(−jϕ).
solution: F₀ = 10 Hz, T = 0.1 s. Harmonics present: k = 0, 1, 3.
a₀ = 3 (the DC term). a₁ = 4, b₁ = 0. 2cos(2π·30t + π/2) = −2 sin(2π·30t), so a₃ = 0, b₃ = −2. All other aₖ, bₖ = 0.
Complex: X₀ = 3. X₁ = X₋₁ = 2. X₃ = (2/2)e^(jπ/2) = j, X₋₃ = e^(−jπ/2) = −j. |X₃| = |X₋₃| = 1.
Magnitude spectrum: lines at 0 Hz (3), ±10 Hz (2 each), ±30 Hz (1 each). Nothing else.
exercises.why: Reading a signal's ingredients off its formula — and predicting the spectrum before you plot it — is the check that catches bugs in every lab notebook. And 'this term is really a sine' is the kind of detail that decides whether a phase spectrum makes sense.

exercises.title: Why multiply-and-integrate finds a coefficient
exercises.prompt: Explain, in your own words and one short calculation, why integrating x(t)·cos(2π·k·F₀·t) over one period picks out only the k-th cosine's amplitude and zeroes out everything else. Use x(t) = a₁cos(2πF₀t) + a₂cos(2π·2F₀t).
hints: Multiply x(t) by cos(2π·2F₀t) and integrate over one period. You get two integrals: a₁∫cos(2πF₀t)cos(2π2F₀t) and a₂∫cos²(2π2F₀t). Think about each separately.

The mistake is trying to compute the integrals from scratch. Use the two facts from the chapter: the integral of a product of *different* harmonics over a period is 0, and the integral of cos² over a period is T/2.
So the a₁ term vanishes (different harmonics) and the a₂ term gives a₂·T/2. Divide by T/2 and you have a₂. That's the recipe: multiply, integrate, normalize.
solution: First integral: different harmonics are orthogonal — it's 0. Second: cos² over a period integrates to T/2.
Intuition: multiplying by the k-th cosine and averaging asks 'how much of x moves in step with this cosine?' Every other harmonic spends as much time in step as out of step, so it averages to zero.
exercises.why: This 'correlate with a template and average' move is the DFT, the matched filter in radar, the way a phone finds a Wi-Fi carrier, and — in LING 124 — how a spectrogram is computed. One idea, everywhere.
